Paired Binary Data

Gosuke Homma

2026-10-26

Source: vignettes/bbssr-paired.Rmd
bbssr-paired.Rmd
library(bbssr)

Design and notation

In a matched-pairs design both treatments are applied to the same unit, as in a cross-over trial, a comparison of two diagnostic procedures on the same patients, or a trial that treats one eye of each patient with each treatment. A pair has one of four outcomes. Let p10p_{10} be the probability that only treatment 1 responds and p01p_{01} the probability that only treatment 2 responds. The difference of the response probabilities of the two treatments is δ=p10−p01\delta = p_{10} - p_{01}, and the probability of a discordant pair is ψ=p10+p01\psi = p_{10} + p_{01}. Among NN pairs, let aa and bb be the numbers of the two kinds of discordant pairs. All tests of the package depend on the data only through (a,b)(a, b).

The Paired* functions follow the Binary* functions for two independent groups: PairedRR(), PairedPower() and PairedSampleSize() for the fixed design, and PairedPowerBSSR(), PairedBSSR(), PairedTypeIErrorBSSR() and PairedAlphaAdjBSSR() for blinded sample size re-estimation.

Tests

Six tests are available. 'McNemar' refers Z=(a−b)/a+bZ = (a - b) / \sqrt{a + b} to the standard normal distribution, and 'McNemar-cc' refers (|a−b|−1)/a+b(|a - b| - 1) / \sqrt{a + b} to it, with the continuity correction of formula (2) of Fagerland et al. (2013), and (a−b−1)/a+b(a - b - 1) / \sqrt{a + b} for a one-sided alternative. 'McNemar-exact' refers aa to the binomial distribution with a+ba + b trials and probability 1/2, and 'McNemar-midP' is its mid-p version (Fagerland et al., 2013). 'McNemar-uncond' orders the outcomes by ZZ and maximizes the null tail probability over ψ\psi (Suissa and Shuster, 1991; Berger and Sidik, 2003), optionally with the Berger-Boos procedure. 'Paired-Score' is the score test of Nam (1997) and Tango (1998) for the null hypothesis δ=−margin\delta = -\text{margin}, which reduces to 'McNemar' with a margin of 0.

The example of Berger and Sidik (2003, Section 4) has n=30n = 30 pairs with x10=11x_{10} = 11 and x01=4x_{01} = 4 and tests p10≤p01p_{10} \le p_{01} against p10>p01p_{10} > p_{01}.

pv <- function(...) attr(PairedRR(N = 30, alpha = 0.05, ...), 'p.value')[12, 5]
p.bs <- c(exact = pv(Test = 'McNemar-exact'),
          asymptotic = pv(Test = 'McNemar'),
          unconditional = pv(Test = 'McNemar-uncond', ref.pvalue = TRUE),
          berger.boos = pv(Test = 'McNemar-uncond', ref.pvalue = TRUE, bb.gamma = 0.0005))
round(p.bs, 4)
#>         exact    asymptotic unconditional   berger.boos 
#>        0.0592        0.0354        0.0494        0.0382

The p-values 0.0592, 0.0354, 0.0494, 0.0382 are those of the tests CB, M, Z and ZCZ_C in Table 3 of Berger and Sidik (2003). The rejection region of a test is a triangle of possible outcomes.

plot(PairedRR(N = 30, alpha = 0.05, Test = 'McNemar-uncond', ref.pvalue = TRUE))

Power and number of pairs

The power is the probability of the rejection region under the multinomial distribution of (a,b,N−a−b)(a, b, N - a - b), computed by enumeration. The normal approximation to the number of pairs is formula (9) of Nam (1997), which is formula (3) of Connor (1987) when the margin is 0. In the example of Connor (1987, p. 210) the response probabilities are 0.8 and 0.7 and ψ=0.3\psi = 0.3, so p10=0.2p_{10} = 0.2 and p01=0.1p_{01} = 0.1.

n.std <- PairedSampleSize(p10 = 0.2, p01 = 0.1, alpha = 0.05, tar.power = 0.9,
                          Test = 'McNemar', method = 'standard')
n.exact <- PairedSampleSize(p10 = 0.2, p01 = 0.1, alpha = 0.05, tar.power = 0.9,
                            Test = 'McNemar-exact')
n.midp <- PairedSampleSize(p10 = 0.2, p01 = 0.1, alpha = 0.05, tar.power = 0.9,
                           Test = 'McNemar-midP')
c(standard = n.std$N, exact = n.exact$N, midp = n.midp$N)
#> standard    exact     midp 
#>      254      269      252

The normal approximation gives 254 pairs, as in Connor (1987). The exact search needs 269 pairs for the exact conditional test and 252 for its mid-p version.

Blinded sample size re-estimation

The number of discordant pairs can be counted without unblinding: a pair is discordant whatever treatment responded. At an interim analysis after n1n_{1} pairs, the blinded estimate of ψ\psi is D1/n1D_{1} / n_{1}, where D1D_{1} is the number of discordant pairs. The assumed difference Delta.A is kept, and the estimate is raised to |ΔA||\Delta_{A}| when it is smaller. The number of pairs is then re-estimated by the normal approximation (ss.method = 'standard'), by the exact search ('exact'), or by the smallest number at which the conditional power given D1D_{1} reaches the target ('conditional.power'), the rule of Schepers et al. (2026). The re-estimation depends on the data only through D1D_{1}, and given the numbers of discordant pairs the direction of each discordant pair is independent of them, so the power is computed exactly.

Schepers et al. (2026) plan the exact conditional test at the two-sided level 0.05 with ΔA=0.15\Delta_{A} = 0.15 and ψ=0.2\psi = 0.2.

plan <- PairedSampleSize(p10 = 0.175, p01 = 0.025, alpha = 0.05, tar.power = 0.8,
                         Test = 'McNemar-exact', alternative = 'two.sided',
                         search = 'smallest')
plan$N
#> [1] 72
res <- PairedPowerBSSR(psi = c(0.15, 0.2, 0.3), Delta.T = 0.15, Delta.A = 0.15,
                       N = plan$N, n.interim = 30, alpha = 0.05, tar.power = 0.8,
                       Test = 'McNemar-exact', alternative = 'two.sided',
                       ss.method = 'conditional.power', N.max = 200)
res
#> Blinded sample size re-estimation for paired binary data
#> 
#>   Test             : McNemar-exact
#>   Alternative      : two.sided
#>   Re-estimation    : conditional power (unrestricted)
#>   Pairs            : N = 72 planned, 30 at the interim analysis
#>   Effect           : assumed 0.15, true 0.15
#>   Alpha            : 0.05, target power 0.8
#> 
#>   psi   p10   p01 power.BSSR power.TRAD    E.N
#>  0.15 0.150 0.000     0.8946     0.9684  63.98
#>  0.20 0.175 0.025     0.7415     0.8056  74.97
#>  0.30 0.225 0.075     0.7443     0.5824 109.72

With ψ=0.3\psi = 0.3 the fixed design of 72 pairs has power 0.582, and the re-estimation design 0.744 with 109.7 pairs on average. With ψ=0.15\psi = 0.15 the fixed design has power 0.968 and the re-estimation design 0.895.

PairedBSSR() performs the re-estimation of a single trial. With 5 discordant pairs among 30 interim pairs:

PairedBSSR(n1 = 30, D1 = 5, Delta.A = 0.15, alpha = 0.05, tar.power = 0.8,
           Test = 'McNemar-exact', alternative = 'two.sided',
           ss.method = 'conditional.power', N.max = 200)
#> Blinded sample size re-estimation from paired interim data
#> 
#>   Test             : McNemar-exact
#>   Alternative      : two.sided
#>   Re-estimation    : conditional power (unrestricted)
#>   Assumed effect   : 0.15
#>   Alpha            : 0.05, target power 0.8
#> 
#> Interim data
#>   Pairs            : n1 = 30, discordant D1 = 5
#>   Discordance      : estimate 0.1667, used 0.1667
#>   Planning values  : p10 = 0.1583, p01 = 0.0083
#> 
#> Re-estimation
#>   Re-estimated N   : 53
#>   Still to enrol   : 23 pairs
#>   Final N          : 53
#>   Power at final N : 0.7499
#>   Conditional power: 0.8077

Type I error rate

The exact conditional test keeps its level after any blinded re-estimation, since the number of pairs in which only treatment 1 responds stays binomial given the total number of discordant pairs (Schepers et al., 2026). The other tests have a type I error rate that depends on ψ\psi, and the re-estimation can change it. PairedTypeIErrorBSSR() computes the rate on the boundary p10=p01p_{10} = p_{01} and certifies its largest value. In the example the final number of pairs is at most 150.

tie <- PairedTypeIErrorBSSR(Delta.A = 0.15, N = plan$N, n.interim = 30, alpha = 0.025,
                            tar.power = 0.8, Test = 'McNemar', ss.method = 'standard',
                            N.max = 150)
attr(tie, 'max')
#>   Design       psi        TIE      bound
#> 1   BSSR 0.9790955 0.02576064 0.02576064
#> 2   TRAD 0.3351974 0.02673970 0.02673970
plot(tie)

The largest type I error rate of the asymptotic McNemar test at the one-sided level 0.025 is 0.0258 for the re-estimation design and 0.0267 for the fixed design. PairedAlphaAdjBSSR() lowers the nominal level until the rate is controlled.

adj <- PairedAlphaAdjBSSR(Delta.A = 0.15, N = plan$N, n.interim = 30, alpha = 0.025,
                          tar.power = 0.8, Test = 'McNemar', ss.method = 'standard',
                          N.max = 150)
adj
#> Adjusted significance level for blinded sample size re-estimation
#> 
#>   Test            : McNemar
#>   Alternative     : greater
#>   Adjusted part   : final analysis only
#>   Maximum         : certified over psi in [0, 1]
#>   Target level    : 0.025
#> 
#>        Design   max.TIE alpha.adj max.TIE.adj
#>          BSSR 0.0257606 0.0242598   0.0246174
#>  Fixed sample 0.0267397 0.0244499   0.0247896

Non-inferiority and equivalence

The score test takes a margin. With alternative = 'greater' and margin = 0.05 it tests δ≤−0.05\delta \le -0.05 against δ>−0.05\delta > -0.05. Nam (1997, Section 5) plans a trial with p01=0.05p_{01} = 0.05, δ0=−0.05\delta_{0} = -0.05 and δ1=0\delta_{1} = 0 at the one-sided level 0.05 with power 0.8.

ni <- PairedSampleSize(p10 = 0.05, p01 = 0.05, alpha = 0.05, tar.power = 0.8,
                       Test = 'Paired-Score', margin = 0.05)
c(normal = attr(ni, 'n.raw'), exact = ni$N)
#>   normal    exact 
#> 273.8196 269.0000

Formula (9) of Nam (1997) gives 273.8 pairs, and the exact power of the score test reaches 0.8 with 269 pairs. With alternative = 'equivalence' and margin = c(lower, upper) the null hypothesis δ≤−lower\delta \le -\text{lower} or δ≥upper\delta \ge \text{upper} is tested by two one-sided score tests. In a re-estimation design the type I error rate is evaluated on both boundaries.

References

Berger, R. L. and Sidik, K. (2003). Exact unconditional tests for a 2 × 2 matched-pairs design. Statistical Methods in Medical Research, 12, 91-108.

Connor, R. J. (1987). Sample size for testing differences in proportions for the paired-sample design. Biometrics, 43, 207-211.

Fagerland, M. W., Lydersen, S. and Laake, P. (2013). The McNemar test for binary matched-pairs data: mid-p and asymptotic are better than exact conditional. BMC Medical Research Methodology, 13, 91.

Nam, J. (1997). Establishing equivalence of two treatments and sample size requirements in matched-pairs design. Biometrics, 53, 1422-1430.

Schepers, M., Brannath, W., Hoffmann, E., Stingl, J. and Schmidtmann, I. (2026). Blinded sample size review for McNemar’s test based on primary and surrogate endpoints. arXiv:2608.17784.

Suissa, S. and Shuster, J. J. (1991). The 2 x 2 matched-pairs trial: exact unconditional design and analysis. Biometrics, 47, 361-372.

Tango, T. (1998). Equivalence test and confidence interval for the difference in proportions for the paired-sample design. Statistics in Medicine, 17, 891-908.
